contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: What is Express Entry and who is it for?

A: Express Entry is Canada's system for managing permanent residence applications under three federal economic programs. It's for skilled workers — whether applying from abroad, already working in Canada, or in a skilled trade — who meet the eligibility criteria for at least one of the three programs.
Q: What's the difference between FSW, CEC, and FST?

A: FSW is for foreign work experience and uses its own 67-point grid before CRS applies. CEC is for candidates with Canadian work experience and has no minimum education requirement. FST is for tradespeople and requires either a job offer or a certificate of qualification.
Q: My CRS score feels too low — is Express Entry still realistic?

A: A lower score may still leave other routes to explore. Category rounds use their own eligibility criteria, and a provincial nomination may add 600 CRS points. Neither category eligibility nor a nomination guarantees an invitation, so compare current program rules with your own evidence before deciding what to pursue.
Q: What happens if I miss the 60-day filing deadline?
A: The invitation lapses and the candidate must re-enter the pool and wait for a new invitation, with no guarantee of receiving one again at the same or a better CRS score.
Q: Do you check provincial nomination options as part of an Express Entry review?
A: Yes — a provincial nomination adds 600 CRS points, which places nearly any nominated candidate above recent draw cutoffs, so eligibility is checked against all ten provinces as standard practice.
Q: What changed to the CRS score calculation after November 2026?

A: On November 3, 2026, IRCC introduced the Labour Market Integration factor and removed the LMIA requirement for Express Entry job offers. The maximum CRS is now 1,270 points. Check IRCC's current criteria and your live profile because existing profiles may take up to two weeks to recalculate.
Q: Can an Express Entry job offer earn CRS points without an LMIA?

A: Since November 3, 2026, a qualifying high-wage job offer may earn points under IRCC's Labour Market Integration factor without an LMIA. The offer must meet IRCC's criteria, and the factor uses either qualifying Canadian work experience or offer points, whichever is higher—not both.

contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: Do I need a job offer to qualify for FSW?

A: No. An offer is not required for FSW eligibility. Since November 3, 2026, a qualifying high-wage offer may earn CRS points under the Labour Market Integration factor. A job offer may also support a proof-of-funds exemption when IRCC's current rules allow.
Q: What counts as 'skilled' work experience for FSW?

A: Work experience must fall under NOC TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 — roughly management, professional, technical, and skilled trades/service occupations, based on Canada's National Occupational Classification system.
Q: What if my grid score is below 67 but my CRS score is strong?

A: The 67-point FSW grid and the CRS score are separate assessments. A candidate must pass the FSW grid to be eligible under this specific program, even with a strong CRS score — though they may still qualify under CEC or FST instead.
Q: How long does an educational credential assessment take?

A: It depends on the organization and how quickly your school sends records. Check the assessor's current timeline and arrange transcripts early; you need the completed assessment details before claiming foreign education points in your Express Entry profile.

contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: Does my work experience need to be full-time?
A: The 1-year requirement is generally calculated in full-time equivalent hours — an equivalent amount of part-time work across a longer period can also qualify.
Q: Can experience gained on a study permit count toward CEC?

A: Generally no — CEC requires experience gained with valid work authorization, such as a co-op work permit, PGWP, or other authorized work permit, not incidental work done on-campus under study permit provisions alone.
Q: What CRS score is realistic for CEC in 2026?

A: There is no fixed CEC cutoff. Scores change from draw to draw, and the November 2026 CRS changes make older results especially poor forecasts. Check the latest IRCC rounds and compare your score with the criteria for each round; eligibility alone does not guarantee an invitation.
Q: Can I apply under both CEC and FSW?
A: A single Express Entry profile is assessed for all programs a candidate is eligible under simultaneously — there's no need to choose one exclusively if requirements for more than one are met.

contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: Do I need a job offer to be nominated?

A: It depends on the stream. Some programs require an eligible job offer, while other routes select candidates based on factors such as work experience, education, occupation, language or a connection to the jurisdiction. Check the exact stream rules before relying on a job offer or assuming one is unnecessary.
Q: Can I apply to more than one province at the same time?

A: Express Entry candidates may receive more than one notification of interest, but can hold only one nomination at a time. Each jurisdiction sets its own application rules, and candidates must genuinely intend to live in the place that nominates them. Review each program’s instructions before submitting more than one application; see IRCC’s [Express Entry nomination guidance](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/provincial-nominees/express-entry/get-confirm-nomination.html).
Q: What's the difference between an aligned and a base PNP stream?

A: An Express Entry-aligned nominee stream is for candidates who also qualify for an Express Entry program. Once the nomination is accepted, IRCC adds 600 CRS points to the profile. A non-Express Entry stream uses a separate permanent-residence application. The Atlantic Immigration Program is a distinct federal pathway, not a base PNP stream.

Q: What's the real difference between inland and outland sponsorship?

A: Inland applications are for couples where the partner is already in Canada, and allow an open work permit during processing. Outland applications are filed while the partner is abroad and can, in some cases, process faster — the right choice depends on the couple's specific circumstances.
Q: What triggers a genuineness refusal?

A: Officers look for consistency across the relationship timeline and credible, well-documented shared-life evidence. Thin documentation or inconsistent details are common triggers, but not automatic disqualifiers if addressed with a strong evidence package.
Q: Is the Parents and Grandparents Program accepting new forms?

A: No. IRCC has paused new interest-to-sponsor forms and invitations until further notice, while it continues processing existing applications. The last intake deadline was October 9, 2025. Check the current IRCC notice for any future update.

Q: Can I just reapply with the same documents?

Q: What's the difference between a reapplication and an appeal?

A: No. A refusal can reflect eligibility, admissibility, missing evidence, credibility concerns or other issues. Read the decision reasons before choosing a response; the available options depend on the application type and deadline.

contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: What does a licensed RCIC actually help with?

A: A Regulated Canadian Immigration Consultant can assess eligibility, develop strategy, prepare and review documentation, represent a client where authorized, and respond when a file becomes complex — always verify registration at the CICC public register before engaging anyone.
Q: Do you only handle Canada-based clients?
A: No — we work with clients applying from anywhere in the world, alongside a sister office in Dubai, UAE serving the wider Commonwealth Migration Group network.
Q: How do I verify your licence?

A: Search RCIC R711256 on the [CICC public register](https://register.college-ic.ca/Public-Register-EN/Licensee/Profile.aspx?ID=14725) before engaging any immigration representative — this applies to any consultant, not just ours.
Q: What information makes an initial immigration review more useful?

A: Share your goal, current status, key deadlines, earlier applications or refusal letters, and the pathway you are considering. The right supporting documents depend on the route, so an initial review should first identify the issue and the dates that control it.

contentBlocks.text: What changed in the Ontario PNP (OINP) in 2026?

Ontario’s first redesign phase took effect on 25 June 2026, replacing eight former streams with the Ontario Workforce Priority stream. The new EOI portal opened on 4 August 2026. On 5 October, Ontario updated the earnings-history score: $80,000 or more in one year within the past five years earns 10 points when supported by a CRA Notice of Assessment. Ontario’s invitations page listed no Workforce Priority round or cutoff as of 9 November 2026; confirm current selection activity before relying on this snapshot.

contentBlocks.text: The closed streams include Employer Job Offer (Foreign Worker, International Student and In-Demand Skills), Master’s Graduate, PhD Graduate, Human Capital Priorities, French-Speaking Skilled Worker and Skilled Trades. Applications already submitted under a former stream are assessed under the rules that applied when filed. Ontario says further changes may follow as the redesign continues, but has not published a launch date; check its updates before registering.

The Ontario PNP has two job-offer pathways and one route without a job offer for eligible self-employed physicians only. Other self-employed applicants cannot use this stream without an employer. Choose the pathway by the job’s NOC TEER category or the physician criteria, then check every applicant and employer requirement before registering an Expression of Interest (EOI).

contentBlocks.text: Ontario PNP eligibility: OINP requirements by pathway

Eligibility depends on the pathway, not simply on having an Ontario job offer or a high EOI score. Job-offer applicants must meet the relevant work-experience, language, education, status and intention rules, and the employer’s position must be approved. The EOI score ranks attributes; it does not replace the minimum eligibility criteria.
OINP TEER 4 and 5 requirements: work experience, CLB and education

items: TEER 0–3: normally 6 consecutive months of paid full-time work in the offered position within the last 12 months; a qualifying recent Ontario graduate may use 3 months in that position; or an applicant may qualify through 2 years of cumulative paid full-time work in the same NOC occupation within 5 years, or a mandatory licence/authorization.
TEER 4–5: at least 9 cumulative months of paid full-time work in the offered position within the last 2 years.
NOC 73300 transport truck drivers and NOC 73301 bus/transit operators must meet the 6-month in-position rule, even if licensed or a recent Ontario graduate.
For full-time work, Ontario generally requires at least 30 paid hours per week. Check the detailed rules for eligible related NOCs, part-time equivalents and interruptions.

contentBlocks.text: OINP language requirements: CLB and IELTS

For TEER 0–3, the usual minimum is CLB 6 in all four abilities, or CLB 5 for a listed skilled trade. TEER 4–5 requires CLB 4. Approved test results must be less than two years old when you apply. A qualifying Ontario graduate may be exempt from the language test for TEER 0–3. The physician pathway has separate criteria.

Approved tests include IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General, PTE Core, TEF Canada and TCF Canada. Confirm accepted test versions and score conversions in the current Ontario instructions before booking or submitting a test.
Education, legal status and intention to live in Ontario

items: TEER 0–3 generally requires post-secondary education of at least one year; listed skilled trades may use a high-school credential. TEER 4–5 requires a secondary-school credential or equivalent.
Use a Canadian credential or the required Educational Credential Assessment (ECA) to establish foreign education and any education points. Check that an ECA meets Ontario’s validity period.
If you are in Canada, you must have legal status when the rules require it. Every applicant must intend to live and work in Ontario after permanent residence.

contentBlocks.text: OINP employer requirements for an Ontario job offer

The employer must qualify before an employee can receive an Ontario nomination under a job-offer pathway. The offer must be full-time (at least 30 paid hours a week and 1,560 hours a year), permanent, urgently necessary to the business and not affect a labour dispute. It must meet the regional median wage, except that a qualifying recent Ontario graduate with a TEER 0–3 offer may use the low-wage level. Ontario also checks operating history, premises, compliance, revenue, staffing and, for some candidates, domestic recruitment.

items: At least 3 years in active business before applying.
A business premises in Ontario where the nominee will work or report to work.
No outstanding orders under the Employment Standards Act, 2000 or the Occupational Health and Safety Act.
At least the required number of full-time Canadian citizen or permanent-resident employees at the relevant work/report location.

The employer must make reasonable domestic recruitment efforts unless the applicant is already authorized to work in Ontario or the employer has a positive LMIA for the same NOC code and position. Ontario may expect at least two recruitment methods and advertisements running for at least four weeks.
For NOC 73300 or 73301 job offers, the employer also needs a valid CVOR and an Excellent or Satisfactory safety rating.

The applicant and family may hold equity only when it was obtained as employee remuneration and their combined ownership is less than 10%; otherwise the equity restriction may make the offer ineligible.
The employee must not pay for a job offer. A non-genuine offer or misrepresentation can lead to refusal and serious immigration consequences.

How to apply for the Ontario PNP (OINP): steps and deadlines

For a job-offer application, the employer acts first. The candidate registers an EOI only after receiving the employer’s job-offer ID. If Ontario issues an invitation, both parties must meet short, separate deadlines. A self-employed physician follows a separate application route.

items: Confirm the current Workforce Priority pathway and minimum eligibility requirements.
For a job offer, the employer registers and submits the position through Ontario’s Employer Portal.
Register the EOI within 30 calendar days of the employer’s job-offer submission. EOI registration is free and remains in the pool for up to 12 months under the current instructions.
If invited, the employer submits the employment-position approval application within 14 calendar days.
After the employer submits, the applicant submits the nomination application and pays within 17 calendar days of the invitation.
If approved, follow the nomination conditions and apply to IRCC for permanent residence within 6 months.

contentBlocks.text: OINP application fee and Express Entry option

The application fee is $2,000 for a job or physician practice location in the GTA and $1,500 outside the GTA; the EOI is free. Federal permanent-residence fees are separate. Eligible TEER 0–3 job-offer candidates and physicians may request an Express Entry-aligned nomination if they meet federal program requirements. Accept the nomination in your Express Entry profile within 30 days; it adds 600 CRS points. If IRCC then invites you, the federal permanent-residence application is due within 60 days.

Q: How long can I use a Canadian visitor visa?

Q: Can a Super Visa lead to permanent residence?

A: No. A Super Visa gives temporary resident status for a visit; it does not lead to permanent residence. A family may consider it separately from an existing PGP case, but IRCC has paused new PGP forms and invitations until further notice.

A: Yes, if the insurer meets IRCC’s requirements. The foreign insurer must be authorized by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions to provide accident and sickness insurance in Canada. The policy must provide at least $100,000 of emergency coverage, cover health care, hospitalization and repatriation, and meet the one-year and payment rules. Q: What income test applies to a Super Visa host in 2026?

A: Since March 31, 2026, the host and co-signer may qualify using income from either of the two tax years before the application. In some cases, the visiting parent or grandparent can contribute income if the host and co-signer meet IRCC’s minimum share. contentBlocks.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Q: How long do I have to file a sponsorship appeal?

A: The IAD must receive the Notice of Appeal and required documents within 30 days after the sponsor receives the refusal decision. Confirm the deadline on the [official appeal page](https://irb-cisr.gc.ca/en/forms/Pages/notice-of-appeal-sponsorship.aspx) and treat it as urgent.
Q: Can I submit new evidence at the appeal that wasn't in my original application?
A: Yes — the IAD can consider new evidence not before the original officer, which is one of the key advantages of the appeal process over simply reapplying.
Q: What happens if the appeal is dismissed?
A: Further options can include an application for leave to the Federal Court, though this is a narrower and more procedural review than the IAD's own hearing.
Q: Who can file a sponsorship appeal?

A: For an eligible refusal of a permanent-resident visa application for a sponsored family member, the sponsor files the appeal; the sponsored person cannot file it. The Immigration Appeal Division explains the [appeal steps and who may appeal](https://irb-cisr.gc.ca/en/making-immigration-appeal/Pages/immapp-a2.aspx).
Q: Can I appeal a refusal of a visitor, study, or work visa for a family member?

A: No. The Immigration Appeal Division’s sponsorship appeal process is for eligible family-class permanent-resident visa refusals, not temporary-resident visa refusals. Confirm the refusal type and the [IAD appeal rules](https://irb-cisr.gc.ca/en/forms/Pages/notice-of-appeal-sponsorship.aspx) immediately because the filing deadline is strict.

Q: Is judicial review the same as an appeal?
